weaknesses: The main split protocol randomly partitions instances without clearly establishing disjoint workflows or task queries. Reconstruction-only, contrastive-only, and within-domain pretraining ablations are also missing.

The utility metric measures top-k set overlap, not ranking order or the actual performance of selected workflows. The value of k and tie handling are unspecified. Workflow-mean and task-only baselines, selection regret, and rank correlation would help establish whether the predictor learns useful workflow–task interactions.

Table 3 provides concrete positive evidence across two workflow frameworks and three domains. Average accuracy improves from the strongest baseline's 78.36% to 79.97%, and utility improves from 73.54% to 76.33%, with three-seed variability reported.

The evaluation includes modality ablations, limited-label experiments, alternative GNN backbones, cross-system and cross-domain tests, and downstream workflow optimization. These provide useful evidence beyond a single prediction benchmark.
Combining graph structure with global code and prompt embeddings is technically plausible, and the full representation achieves the best average results in the modality ablation.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is incremental relative to FLORA's workflow predictors and established multimodal/self-supervised representation learning. The framework combines standard GNNs, attention, MLP fusion, reconstruction, and contrastive objectives, without sufficiently isolating which new mechanism explains the gains. Parameter-matched baselines receiving the same input information and simpler fusion alternatives are needed.

The main split protocol does not establish generalization to unseen workflows. Section 4.1 randomly splits instances, although many instances share workflows and tasks. Appendix B.5 simultaneously claims that no validation/test workflows enter pretraining, without explaining how workflow separation is enforced. Its 232,104 samples also greatly exceed the number of unique workflows, making deduplication and repeated-workflow handling important. Explicit workflow-disjoint and task-disjoint evaluations, alongside workflow-average and task-only baselines, would clarify what is learned.

The utility metric is top-k set overlap, not a measure of ordering within the selected set or achieved workflow performance. The chosen k and tie handling are unspecified. Without random-overlap reference values, rank correlation, or selection regret, the practical meaning of the reported utility scores is difficult to assess.

The pretraining study does not isolate the claimed cross-domain benefit. There are no matched within-domain versus cross-domain comparisons or separate reconstruction/contrastive ablations. The pretraining pool is approximately 90.58% reasoning samples, and repeated workflow embeddings may become false negatives under the stated contrastive sampling procedure.

The efficiency claims omit material costs. The 110–120-evaluation break-even estimate includes predictor training but excludes acquiring labeled executions and does not clearly account for text/code embedding computation. Table 13 reports zero search cost while explicitly excluding candidate-update LLM calls. End-to-end costs and performance under matched total budgets are needed to support the central savings claim.

Downstream results substantially qualify the conclusions. Table 13 reports 74.43% average performance versus 84.23% for execution-based AFlow. On HotpotQA, the proposed method achieves 13.37%, below random search's 16.86% and far below AFlow's 69.94%; describing this as notable transferability or broadly comparable performance is unsupported. Search experiments also omit stronger predictor baselines such as GCN-II and Graph Transformer and report no uncertainty.

Several architectural claims exceed the ablation evidence. Multi-graph encoding increases average utility only from 78.72% to 78.75%, while adding some modality pairs sharply reduces performance. These patterns deserve investigation rather than a uniformly positive interpretation. Collectively, the unresolved evaluation and cost-accounting issues prevent the otherwise promising benchmark improvements from establishing a contribution competitive for acceptance.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing expensive execution-based evaluation during agentic workflow search. Combining graph structure, code, prompts, and task context is well motivated.

Table 3 reports consistent improvements across six domain/framework settings, with average accuracy of 79.97% and utility of 76.33%, exceeding the strongest baseline averages by 1.61 and 2.79 percentage points, respectively. Three-seed variability is reported.

The evaluation includes modality ablations, limited-label experiments, alternative backbones, cross-framework and cross-domain tests, and downstream workflow optimization. These provide useful evidence beyond prediction accuracy alone.
Downstream optimization improves average task performance over GCN and GAT predictors, and the compact prediction head offers a promising way to amortize evaluation costs.
weaknesses: The main split does not establish generalization to unseen workflows. Section 4.1 randomly splits instances, although many instances share workflow configurations and task queries. Appendix B.5 claims that validation/test workflows are excluded from pretraining without explaining how this is reconciled with instance-level splitting. Explicit workflow-disjoint, task-disjoint, and jointly disjoint splits are needed; the OOD experiments are useful but do not resolve this ambiguity.

Novelty beyond FLORA is incremental: the central additions combine established multi-view fusion, pretrained code/text embeddings, and standard reconstruction/contrastive objectives. Comparisons do not adequately isolate richer input information and model capacity from the proposed architecture. A simple capacity-matched predictor receiving all the same embeddings, alongside task-only and historical workflow-success baselines, would be particularly informative.

The evidence for cross-domain pretraining is incomplete. There are no reconstruction-only, contrastive-only, or within-domain pretraining controls. The claimed 232,104 pretraining samples substantially exceed the number of unique workflows in Table 2, and sampling explicitly uses no deduplication. Repeated configurations could become false negatives in the instance-based contrastive objective; their treatment is unspecified.

Utility measures top-k set overlap, not ordering within the selected set or achieved execution quality. The value of k and tie handling are not specified, preventing reliable interpretation or reproduction. Selection regret, rank correlation, and performance-versus-evaluation-budget curves would better substantiate the search claims.

Efficiency accounting is incomplete. The 0.054 ms inference figure does not clearly include code/text embedding computation for new candidates, while the break-even calculation excludes label acquisition. Appendix B.6 explicitly excludes workflow-generation calls from its reported zero search cost. These measurements therefore do not establish end-to-end savings for a new deployment.

The transferability claims overstate the downstream evidence. Table 13 reports 74.43% average performance versus 84.23% for execution-based AFlow. HotpotQA performance is 13.37%, below random selection at 16.86%, GAT at 21.47%, and AFlow at 69.94%; describing this as notable transferability is unconvincing. Downstream results also lack uncertainty estimates and comparisons against several stronger predictor baselines.
